h1: What is new in brewing in 2026: the trends worth watching
title: What Is New in Brewing in 2026 | Craft Beer School
desc: Alcohol-free beer, clean lagers, hop water, new hops, climate and AI: the brewing trends of 2026 explained in plain language for beer lovers.
teaser: Alcohol-free beer is growing, lager is back in fashion and brewers are worried about the weather. Here is what is actually changing.
standfirst: Beer is changing faster than most drinkers notice. We pick the trends that have real numbers behind them and explain each one in plain language, from alcohol-free beer to the hot summer that hit German hop farms.
sections: Alcohol-free beer is the growth story

Across the world people are drinking a little less. More of what they drink has no alcohol at all. The drinks research firm IWSR said in June 2026 that alcohol-free beer grew 8% by volume in 2025. It expects that kind of beer to double its share of the world's beer, from 2% to 4%, by 2033. Total beer, meanwhile, is forecast to slip about 1% over the next decade.

Good alcohol-free beer is hard to make. Take the alcohol out and you lose body and aroma too, so brewers now use special yeasts and gentler methods to keep the flavour. In the US, Circana figures quoted by Constellation Brands put alcohol-free beer sales up 22% in 2025. If you have tried one recently and been surprised how much it tastes like beer, that work is why.

After years of ever-stranger IPAs, many brewers are going back to clean, crisp beer done well. Escarpment Labs, a Canadian yeast maker, put it simply in its predictions for 2026: better over new. It also expects more small brewers to pasteurise light lagers and alcohol-free beers, to keep them fresh and safe on the shelf.

Fruit is coming back too, this time in clean lagers and wheat beers rather than sour ones, where it sits in the background instead of shouting. Watch for the cold IPA as well, a hoppy beer brewed with lager yeast and a little rice or maize for a dry, crisp finish. Our cold IPA guide explains it.

Hop water is sparkling water flavoured with hops: no alcohol, no sugar, almost no calories. It boomed a few years ago and has since cooled. NielsenIQ data reported by Food Dive showed US hop water sales falling 7.3% in the year to late October 2025, while alcohol-free beer grew 18%. Big brewers still see a future in it. In March 2026 Constellation Brands bought the hop water brand Hopwtr.

The same mood is behind lower-calorie and lower-strength beers: something to drink with friends that does not wreck the next morning.

Hops give beer its bitterness and much of its smell. Breeders released around ten new varieties in the past year, with names like Dolcita, Luna and Rhapzody, many tasting of mango, peach and passionfruit. We list them in new hop varieties for 2026. Brewers are also using hop oils and liquids in place of dried pellets, which wastes less beer.
The weather is now a brewing problem

Beer starts on a farm. Farms are feeling the heat. This summer Bavaria recorded 40.8 °C and Germany's hop crop is expected to be 22% smaller than last year, according to the Brewers Association. Some of the classic hops in German lagers were hit hardest. That is why breeders now pick new hops for heat and drought tolerance as much as flavour. Saving water and energy in the brewery is part of the same story. HVG, the German hop growers' co-operative, says in its 2025 sustainability report that it is breeding for drought tolerance and for hops that need less spraying and fertiliser. Lager drinkers in Bengaluru will taste the results of that work within a few years.

Artificial intelligence is arriving in breweries, mostly in quiet ways. An October 2026 report describes brewers using it to watch fermentations, plan production and spot problems early. A few have gone further. In Japan, NEC and COEDO Brewery used AI to help design a beer series in 2025. A person still brews the beer and decides whether it is any good.
What it means for beer lovers in India

India is one of the few places where drinking is still growing. IWSR forecasts Indian servings to rise 38% between 2025 and 2035, with India passing the US in 2032 to become the second-largest drinks market by servings. Expect more alcohol-free options, more well-made lagers alongside the wheat beers and a growing number of brewpubs that can tell you which hop is in your glass. If you want to know how they do it, our guide to craft beer in India is a good next read.
